claim: Homotypic or entotic cell-in-cell invasion is an integrin-independent process observed in carcinoma cells exposed during conditions of low adhesion such as in exudates of malignant disease.
source: Homotypic or entotic cell-in-cell invasion is an integrin-independent process observed in carcinoma cells exposed during conditions of low adhesion such as in exudates of malignant disease.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established knowledge about entosis and its characteristics in cancer cells.

claim: Active cell-in-cell invasion depends on RhoA and actin.
source: Although active cell-in-cell invasion depends on RhoA and actin, the precise mechanism as well as the underlying actin structures and assembly factors driving the process are unknown.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about the dependence of entosis on RhoA and actin.

claim: The G-protein-coupled LPA receptor 2 (LPAR2) is a signal transducer specifically required for the actively invading cell during entosis.
source: In this study, we identify the G-protein-coupled LPA receptor 2 (LPAR2) as a signal transducer specifically required for the actively invading cell during entosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: G12/13 and PDZ-RhoGEF are required for entotic invasion.
source: We find that G12/13 and PDZ-RhoGEF are required for entotic invasion, which is driven by blebbing and a uropod-like actin structure at the rear of the invading cell.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Entotic invasion is driven by blebbing and a uropod-like actin structure at the rear of the invading cell.
source: We find that G12/13 and PDZ-RhoGEF are required for entotic invasion, which is driven by blebbing and a uropod-like actin structure at the rear of the invading cell.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 1 and videos.

claim: The RhoA-regulated formin Dia1 is involved in entosis downstream of LPAR2.
source: Finally, we provide evidence for an involvement of the RhoA-regulated formin Dia1 for entosis downstream of LPAR2.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Entosis is a specialized form of homotypic cell-in-cell invasion in which one cell actively crawls into another.
source: Entosis has been described as a specialized form of homotypic cell-in-cell invasion in which one cell actively crawls into another (Overholtzer et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Overholtzer et al., 2007.

claim: Entosis occurs between tumor cells such as breast, cervical, or colon carcinoma cells.
source: Frequently, this occurs between tumor cells such as breast, cervical, or colon carcinoma cells and can be triggered by matrix detachment (Overholtzer et al., 2007), suggesting that loss of integrin-mediated adhesion may promote cell-in-cell invasion.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Overholtzer et al., 2007.

claim: Entosis can be triggered by matrix detachment.
source: Frequently, this occurs between tumor cells such as breast, cervical, or colon carcinoma cells and can be triggered by matrix detachment (Overholtzer et al., 2007), suggesting that loss of integrin-mediated adhesion may promote cell-in-cell invasion.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Overholtzer et al., 2007.

claim: Loss of integrin-mediated adhesion may promote cell-in-cell invasion.
source: Frequently, this occurs between tumor cells such as breast, cervical, or colon carcinoma cells and can be triggered by matrix detachment (Overholtzer et al., 2007), suggesting that loss of integrin-mediated adhesion may promote cell-in-cell invasion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that matrix detachment triggers entosis.

claim: Homotypic cell-in-cell structures can be regularly found when tumor cells are released into fluid exudates such as ascites or during pleural carcinosis.
source: This is further supported by the fact that homotypic cell-in-cell structures can be regularly found when tumor cells are released into fluid exudates such as ascites or during pleural carcinosis (Overholtzer and Brugge, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Overholtzer and Brugge, 2008.

claim: Entosis may contribute to tumor progression by inducing aneuploidy in human cancers.
source: Although the consequence of entotic invasion is not well understood, the process may contribute to tumor progression by inducing aneuploidy in human cancers (Krajcovic et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Krajcovic et al., 2011.

claim: The invaded cell can remain viable or even divide inside or escape from the host cell or undergo vacuolar degradation.
source: The ultimate outcome of an entotic event also depends on the fate of the invaded cell, which can remain viable or even divide inside or escape from the host cell or undergo vacuolar degradation (Florey et al., 2010; Krajcovic et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Florey et al., 2010 and Krajcovic et al., 2011.

claim: For a cell to invade into a neighboring cell, Rho-dependent signaling and actin are required.
source: It was previously shown that for a cell to invade into a neighboring cell Rho-dependent signaling and actin are required (Overholtzer et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Overholtzer et al., 2007.

claim: Potential extracellular ligands or cell surface receptors involved in entotic invasion are entirely unknown.
source: However, potential extracellular ligands or cell surface receptors involved in this migratory process are entirely unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The type of actin structures and which actin polymerization factor triggers active cell-in-cell invasion in a signal-regulated fashion remained unclear.
source: Furthermore, what type of actin structures and which actin polymerization factor triggers active cell-in-cell invasion in a signal-regulated fashion remained unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The actively invading cell displays extensive blebbing early on during invasion followed by the formation of an actin-rich uropod-like structure at the rear of the invading cell.
source: Interestingly, imaging LifeAct-expressing cells over time, we consistently observed that specifically the actively invading cell displayed extensive blebbing early on during invasion followed by the formation of an actin-rich uropod-like structure at the rear of the invading cell (Figure 1A; Video 2).
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A and Video 2.

claim: Cell-in-cell invasion requires ROCK.
source: Under these conditions, cell-in-cell invasion was confirmed to require ROCK as assessed using the ROCK-inhibitor Y-27632 (Video 1) (Overholtzer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data using ROCK inhibitor shown in Video 1 and supported by citation.

claim: Plasma membrane blebbing is highly dynamic under non-adhesive cell culture conditions with a bleb cycle lasting about 2 min.
source: Plasma membrane blebbing was highly dynamic under these cell culture conditions with a bleb cycle lasting about 2 min (Figure 1B; Video 3) and the total number of blebs ranged from 60 to 100 blebs per cell depending on the MCF10A cell size.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation supported by data in Figure 1B and Video 3.

claim: The total number of blebs ranged from 60 to 100 blebs per cell depending on the MCF10A cell size.
source: Plasma membrane blebbing was highly dynamic under these cell culture conditions with a bleb cycle lasting about 2 min (Figure 1B; Video 3) and the total number of blebs ranged from 60 to 100 blebs per cell depending on the MCF10A cell size.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation supported by data in Figure 1B and Video 3.

claim: Blebbing is a frequently observed phenomenon during amoeboid or rounded cancer cell invasion through 3-dimensional collagen requiring ROCK-dependent contractility.
source: Notably, blebbing is a frequently observed phenomenon during amoeboid or rounded cancer cell invasion through 3-dimensional collagen requiring ROCK-dependent contractility (Sahai and Marshall, 2003; Kitzing et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sahai and Marshall, 2003 and Kitzing et al., 2007.

claim: LPA stimulates entosis in MCF10A cells under serum-free conditions in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, under serum-free conditions addition of LPA efficiently stimulated entotic events of MCF10A cells in a concentration-dependent manner already at nanomolar concentrations (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The LPA-receptor 1, 2 and 3 inhibitor Ki16425 completely blocks LPA-stimulated entosis.
source: This ligand mediated cell-in-cell invasion was dependent on cell surface receptor activity since the LPA-receptor 1, 2 and 3 inhibitor Ki16425 completely blocked LPA-stimulated entosis (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Ki16425 blocks serum-stimulated entosis.
source: Comparable results were obtained when entosis was triggered by serum (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: LPA is a soluble extracellular ligand and serum component that mediates cell-in-cell invasion.
source: These data identify the soluble extracellular ligand and serum component LPA as a mediator of cell-in-cell invasion.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing LPA stimulates entosis.

claim: LPA transduces its multiple cellular effects via binding to specific LPA-receptors, which belong to the large superfamily of G-protein-coupled receptors.
source: LPA transduces its multiple cellular effects via binding to specific LPA-receptors, which belong to the large superfamily of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about LPA receptor signaling.

claim: Silencing of LPAR2 results in a robust and significant reduction of entotic events.
source: Interestingly, silencing of LPAR2 resulted in a robust and significant reduction of entotic events, while LPAR5 suppression moderately affected entosis (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LPAR5 suppression moderately affects entosis.
source: Interestingly, silencing of LPAR2 resulted in a robust and significant reduction of entotic events, while LPAR5 suppression moderately affected entosis (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LPAR2 is specifically required for the actively invading cell and not for the host cell during entosis.
source: Examination of entotic events using confocal fluorescence microscopy revealed that only cells silenced for LPAR2 failed to actively invade into another, while LPAR2 suppression did not inhibit the host cell during this process (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the two-color entosis assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Transient expression of LPAR2 in HEK293 cells significantly triggers entotic invasion.
source: Notably, transient expression of LPAR2 in HEK293 cells significantly triggered entotic invasion (Figure 2C), suggesting that disease-associated overexpression or upregulation of LPAR2 as observed in various human cancers (Goetzl et al., 1999; Kitayama et al., 2004; Yun et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2007) may be instrumental for entosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Disease-associated overexpression or upregulation of LPAR2 is observed in various human cancers.
source: Notably, transient expression of LPAR2 in HEK293 cells significantly triggered entotic invasion (Figure 2C), suggesting that disease-associated overexpression or upregulation of LPAR2 as observed in various human cancers (Goetzl et al., 1999; Kitayama et al., 2004; Yun et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2007) may be instrumental for entosis.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Goetzl et al., 1999; Kitayama et al., 2004; Yun et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2007.

claim: Overexpression or upregulation of LPAR2 may be instrumental for entosis.
source: Notably, transient expression of LPAR2 in HEK293 cells significantly triggered entotic invasion (Figure 2C), suggesting that disease-associated overexpression or upregulation of LPAR2 as observed in various human cancers (Goetzl et al., 1999; Kitayama et al., 2004; Yun et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2007) may be instrumental for entosis.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that LPAR2 expression triggers entosis and is upregulated in cancers.

claim: Endogenous LPAR2 shows a cortical signal that is distinctively increased at the rear of the invading cell during more progressed phase of entotic invasion.
source: Staining of cells with anti-LPAR2 antibodies showed a cortical signal that was distinctively increased at the rear of the invading cell in particular during more progressed phase of entotic invasion (Figure 2D), which could be confirmed on transiently expressed Flag-LPAR2 (Figure 2E), suggesting that LPAR2-signaling occurs in a defined and more polarized manner.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: LPAR2-signaling occurs in a defined and more polarized manner.
source: Staining of cells with anti-LPAR2 antibodies showed a cortical signal that was distinctively increased at the rear of the invading cell in particular during more progressed phase of entotic invasion (Figure 2D), which could be confirmed on transiently expressed Flag-LPAR2 (Figure 2E), suggesting that LPAR2-signaling occurs in a defined and more polarized manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the polarized localization of LPAR2 shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Flag-LPAR2 polarization to the trailing cell rear is independent of downstream actin organization.
source: Flag-LPAR2 polarization to the trailing cell rear was independent of downstream actin organization as assessed by addition of latrunculin B, which completely perturbed the cortical actin cytoskeleton (Figure 2E, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using latrunculin B shown in Figure 2E.

claim: LPAR2 can initiate intracellular signaling via coupling to multiple Gα subunits from the Gi, Gq, and G12/13 family of heterotrimeric G-proteins.
source: LPAR2 can initiate intracellular signaling via coupling to multiple Gα subunits from the Gi, Gq, and G12/13 family of heterotrimeric G-proteins (Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Choi et al., 2010.

claim: Suppression of Gα12/13 effectively and significantly blocks entosis.
source: Silencing various Gα subunits by siRNA revealed that only suppression of Gα12/13 effectively and significantly blocked entosis (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LPAR2-triggered entotic invasion specifically requires Gα12/13, but not Gα11 or Gαq.
source: Consistently, LPAR2-triggered entotic invasion specifically required Gα12/13, but not Gα11 or Gαq (Figure 3B), clearly demonstrating that LPAR2 signals through G12/13 heterotrimeric G-proteins to promote homotypic cell-in-cell invasion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LPAR2 signals through G12/13 heterotrimeric G-proteins to promote homotypic cell-in-cell invasion.
source: Consistently, LPAR2-triggered entotic invasion specifically required Gα12/13, but not Gα11 or Gαq (Figure 3B), clearly demonstrating that LPAR2 signals through G12/13 heterotrimeric G-proteins to promote homotypic cell-in-cell invasion.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing Gα12/13 requirement.

claim: Expression of Gα12 or of a constitutively active mutant Gα12Q/L robustly induces entotic events in the absence of LPA.
source: Furthermore, expression of Gα12 or of a constitutively active mutant Gα12Q/L robustly induced entotic events in the absence of LPA, and this effect was further increased upon addition of 2 μM LPA (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A canonical LPAR2/Gα12/13 module critically mediates entosis.
source: Thus, a canonical LPAR2/ Gα12/13 module critically mediates entosis.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing LPAR2 and Gα12/13 requirements.

claim: Gα12/13 proteins directly relay receptor signal informations by binding to the RGS-domain containing RhoGEFs p115-rhoGEF, LARG, or PDZ-RhoGEF for activation of the small GTPase RhoA.
source: Gα12/13 proteins have been shown to directly relay receptor signal informations by binding to the RGS-domain containing RhoGEFs p115-rhoGEF, LARG, or PDZ-RhoGEF (Fukuhara et al., 2001) for activation of the small GTPase RhoA (Fukuhara et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fukuhara et al., 2001.

claim: siRNA-mediated knock-down of PDZ-RhoGEF specifically inhibits entotic events.
source: Interestingly, siRNA-mediated knock-down of PDZ-RhoGEF specifically inhibited entotic events (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ectopically expressed GFP-PDZ-RhoGEF shows a strikingly polarized distribution to the invading cell rear where it strongly colocalizes with F-actin.
source: Furthermore, analyzing ectopically expressed GFP-PDZ-RhoGEF during cell-in-cell invasion revealed a strikingly polarized distribution to the invading cell rear where it strongly colocalized with F-actin as determined by LifeAct (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Phosphorylated myosin-light-chain II (pMLC2) is enriched at the trailing cell rear during entosis.
source: Similar observations were made by staining for phosphorylated myosin-light-chain II (pMLC2) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), a downstream target of the Rho-ROCK pathway, in agreement with previous findings (Wan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation.

claim: pMLC2 is a downstream target of the Rho-ROCK pathway.
source: Similar observations were made by staining for phosphorylated myosin-light-chain II (pMLC2) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), a downstream target of the Rho-ROCK pathway, in agreement with previous findings (Wan et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wan et al., 2012.

claim: PDZ-RhoGEF promotes localized actin assembly at the cell rear during entotic invasion.
source: These data argue that PDZ-RhoGEF promotes localized actin assembly at the cell rear during entotic invasion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and knockdown data for PDZ-RhoGEF.

claim: During entosis the invading but not the receiving cells display rigorous membrane blebbing.
source: Our LifeAct or non-transfected cell analysis showed that during entosis the invading but not the receiving cells display rigorous membrane blebbing (Figure 1A; Video 2) reminiscent of bleb-associated cancer cell invasion (Fackler and Grosse, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A and Video 2.

claim: Bleb-associated cancer cell invasion through collagen matrices requires the activity of the Diaphanous formin mDia1 downstream of RhoA.
source: We have shown previously that bleb-associated cancer cell invasion through collagen matrices requires the activity of the Diaphanous formin mDia1 downstream of RhoA (Kitzing et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kitzing et al., 2007.

claim: Endogenous mDia1 is enriched at the cell rear of the invading cell.
source: Interestingly, we found endogenous mDia1 to be enriched at the cell rear of the invading cell (Figure 4A), suggesting that mDia1 function spatially controls entosis.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: mDia1 function spatially controls entosis.
source: Interestingly, we found endogenous mDia1 to be enriched at the cell rear of the invading cell (Figure 4A), suggesting that mDia1 function spatially controls entosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization of mDia1 at the cell rear.

claim: Ectopically expressed mDia1-GFP localizes to the actin-rich cup formed in HEK293 cells upon LPAR2 transfection to trigger entotic invasion.
source: Indeed, ectopically expressed mDia1-GFP was localized to the actin-rich cup formed in HEK293 cells upon LPAR2 transfection to trigger entotic invasion (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: mDia1 is required for Ezrin-positive bleb formation.
source: Analyzing the cells silenced for mDia1, we found that mDia1 was required for Ezrin-positive bleb formation as well as blebbing (Figure 4C,D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Video 3), while mDia1 was localized to cellular blebs in control silenced cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D, E and supplementary figure and video.

claim: mDia1 is required for blebbing.
source: Analyzing the cells silenced for mDia1, we found that mDia1 was required for Ezrin-positive bleb formation as well as blebbing (Figure 4C,D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Video 3), while mDia1 was localized to cellular blebs in control silenced cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D, E and supplementary figure and video.

claim: mDia1 is localized to cellular blebs in control silenced cells.
source: Analyzing the cells silenced for mDia1, we found that mDia1 was required for Ezrin-positive bleb formation as well as blebbing (Figure 4C,D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Video 3), while mDia1 was localized to cellular blebs in control silenced cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Blebbing is highly sensitive to LPAR inhibition with Ki16425.
source: Similarly, blebbing was highly sensitive to LPAR inhibition with Ki16425 (Figure 4F; Video 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Videos 4 and 5.

claim: mDia1 knockdown MCF10A cells are strongly impaired to undergo entotic invasion.
source: Importantly, mDia1 knockdown MCF10A cells were strongly impaired to undergo entotic invasion as compared to control siRNA-treated cells (Figure 4G,H; Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G, H and Video 6.

claim: Addition of latrunculin B just before completion of entosis leads to rapid dispersion of the trailing actin-rich cup and failure of cell-in-cell invasion.
source: Under these conditions, when latrunculin B was added just before completion of entosis, we observed the rapid dispersion of the trailing actin-rich cup leading to failure of cell-in-cell invasion (Figure 4G; Video 6), pointing towards a crucial role for polarized actin assembly during final stages of entosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and Video 6.

claim: Polarized actin assembly plays a crucial role during final stages of entosis.
source: Under these conditions, when latrunculin B was added just before completion of entosis, we observed the rapid dispersion of the trailing actin-rich cup leading to failure of cell-in-cell invasion (Figure 4G; Video 6), pointing towards a crucial role for polarized actin assembly during final stages of entosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that disrupting actin prevents completion of entosis.

claim: Suppression of mDia1 by siRNA treatment strongly and specifically inhibits LPAR2-triggered entosis in HEK293 cells.
source: Suppression of mDia1 by siRNA treatment also strongly and specifically inhibited LPAR2-triggered entosis (Figure 4I) in HEK293 cells, showing that mDia1 is an essential factor that acts downstream of LPAR2 during cell-in-cell invasion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: mDia1 is an essential factor that acts downstream of LPAR2 during cell-in-cell invasion.
source: Suppression of mDia1 by siRNA treatment also strongly and specifically inhibited LPAR2-triggered entosis (Figure 4I) in HEK293 cells, showing that mDia1 is an essential factor that acts downstream of LPAR2 during cell-in-cell invasion.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing mDia1 requirement for LPAR2-triggered entosis.

claim: Homotypic cell-in-cell structures have been reported in metastatic carcinoma cells harvested from exudates or urine samples.
source: Homotypic cell-in-cell structures have been reported in metastatic carcinoma cells harvested from exudates or urine samples (Overholtzer and Brugge, 2008), corresponding to the non-adhesive experimental culture conditions on hydrogel.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Overholtzer and Brugge, 2008.

claim: Active invasive cell-in-cell process may result in some survival advantage or even represent an escape mechanism for carcinoma cells.
source: It is tempting to speculate that such active invasive and complex process may result in some survival advantage or even represent an escape mechanism for carcinoma cells, although often the inner cell undergoes a cell death process involving components of the autophagy machinery (Florey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential biological significance of entosis.

claim: Often the inner cell undergoes a cell death process involving components of the autophagy machinery.
source: It is tempting to speculate that such active invasive and complex process may result in some survival advantage or even represent an escape mechanism for carcinoma cells, although often the inner cell undergoes a cell death process involving components of the autophagy machinery (Florey et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Florey et al., 2011.

claim: Some components of entotic invasion such as RhoA and mDia1 function during rounded cancer cell invasion, which is similarly accompanied by cell blebbing.
source: Interestingly, some of these components such as RhoA and mDia1 have been shown to function during rounded cancer cell invasion, which is similarly accompanied by cell blebbing (Sanz-Moreno and Marshall, 2010), although this processes can still depend on integrin-based matrix adhesions.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sanz-Moreno and Marshall, 2010.

claim: Rounded cancer cell invasion can still depend on integrin-based matrix adhesions.
source: Interestingly, some of these components such as RhoA and mDia1 have been shown to function during rounded cancer cell invasion, which is similarly accompanied by cell blebbing (Sanz-Moreno and Marshall, 2010), although this processes can still depend on integrin-based matrix adhesions.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of rounded cancer cell invasion.

claim: Entotic invasion, although independent of integrins, resembles at least in some aspects that of amoeboid and bleb-dependent motility.
source: Our findings suggest that entotic invasion, although independent of integrins, resembles at least in some aspects that of amoeboid and bleb-dependent motility.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarities observed between entosis and amoeboid invasion.

claim: Actin filaments coincide at the Ezrin-rich uropod in amoeboid blebbing thereby pushing cells through collagen-I.
source: Indeed, actin filaments also coincide at the Ezrin-rich uropod in amoeboid blebbing thereby pushing cells through collagen-I (Lorentzen et al., 2011) and ezrin is further an essential component for non-apoptotic blebbing (Charras et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lorentzen et al., 2011.

claim: Ezrin is an essential component for non-apoptotic blebbing.
source: Indeed, actin filaments also coincide at the Ezrin-rich uropod in amoeboid blebbing thereby pushing cells through collagen-I (Lorentzen et al., 2011) and ezrin is further an essential component for non-apoptotic blebbing (Charras et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Charras et al., 2006.

claim: Ezrin is potentially required for entosis.
source: It seems reasonably that Ezrin is potentially also required for entosis as we observed strong Ezrin localization at the invading cell uropod (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), however, its precise role and regulation in this process remains a future task for investigations.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation of Ezrin localization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Strong Ezrin localization is observed at the invading cell uropod.
source: It seems reasonably that Ezrin is potentially also required for entosis as we observed strong Ezrin localization at the invading cell uropod (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), however, its precise role and regulation in this process remains a future task for investigations.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The relevance of entosis for tumor progression in vivo is currently unclear.
source: The relevance of entosis for tumor progression in vivo is currently unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding entosis.

claim: LPA and LPAR2 are important factors during cancer metastasis.
source: Nevertheless, our data uncover LPA and LPAR2 as important drivers of entotic invasion, both of which are also important factors during cancer metastasis, suggesting that entosis may be a phenomenon associated with advanced malignancy.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LPA and LPAR2 in cancer.

claim: Entosis may be a phenomenon associated with advanced malignancy.
source: Nevertheless, our data uncover LPA and LPAR2 as important drivers of entotic invasion, both of which are also important factors during cancer metastasis, suggesting that entosis may be a phenomenon associated with advanced malignancy.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the involvement of LPA and LPAR2 in both entosis and cancer metastasis.

claim: High fetal calf serum (FCS) concentrations enhance entosis.
source: We noticed that high fetal calf serum (FCS) concentrations enhance entosis (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation made by the authors but data is not shown.

claim: LPA is present at micromolar concentrations in FCS.
source: A ligand known to be present at micromolar concentrations in FCS is lysophosphatidic acid (LPA).
evidence: This is established knowledge about LPA concentration in serum.

claim: The host cell nucleus typically has a half-moon shape during cell-in-cell invasion.
source: One phenotypic hallmark characterizing the host cell from the invading cell during cell-in-cell invasion is the typically half-moon-shaped nucleus (Figure 1C; Overholtzer and Brugge, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1C and citation to Overholtzer and Brugge, 2008.
